items.question: What do you see as a fundamental limitation of reinforcement learning?
items.object: Reinforcement learning
items.answer: I think one of the fundamental limitations of RL is that you don't actually know if the model has learned the thing you want to teach it, right? You have no guarantees that the model has learned what you have taught it.
quotes: One of the fundamental limitations of RL is that you don't actually know if the model has learned the thing you want to teach it, right? You have no guarantees that the model has learned what you have taught it.

rubrics.text: The response identifies a fundamental limitation of reinforcement learning as the lack of a guarantee that the model has learned what its trainers intended it to learn.

items.question: How do you understand the problem that reinforcement learning with human feedback was originally meant to solve?
items.object: The original motivation for reinforcement learning with human feedback
items.answer: Actually, in 2018 I was working at OpenAI, so that's when they just started this RLHF. This RLHF idea at the time, in 2018, was that RL agents would often exploit your environment. They would exploit parts of the environment that you really would not want them to. Maybe you wanted to complete this race course, but it finds that it gets a lot of points by looping around the ship. So instead of completing the race course, it will end up looping around the ship an infinite number of times. Initially, the goal was that by having humans give feedback to our agents when playing these interactive games, you could prevent the agents from doing very odd behaviors.

items.question: Why do you think reinforcement learning supervision appealed to researchers working on early language models at OpenAI?
items.object: Applying reinforcement learning supervision to early language models
items.answer: Around 2018 was when the first GPT model came out, so then there was the safety team at OpenAI. I remember there were several people who were interested in the idea that you could use this idea of RL supervision to train the language models to summarize or to have humor, because these are things that are very hard to teach the language model if you just gave it a bunch of internet text. I guess that might have been the start of this idea.

items.question: How do you understand the role of reinforcement learning with human feedback in improving language model behavior?
items.object: Reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF)
items.answer: My understanding of RLHF is that your model will generate different outputs, and then you'll have people rate them. People will say, “This is very desirable; this is not desirable,” and then this gives the model supervision on whether it should generate this output more often or less often. Since these language models have blown up and hallucination is such an obvious problem, people have been using RLHF to guide the models into better behavior.
quotes: The idea of RLHF is that your model will generate different outputs, and then you'll have people rate them. People will say, “This is very desirable; this is not desirable,” and then this gives the model supervision on whether it should generate this output more often or less often. Since these language models have blown up and hallucination is such an obvious problem, people have been using RLHF to guide the models into better behavior.

rubrics.text: The response explains that RLHF uses human desirability ratings of model outputs as supervision to make preferred outputs more likely to be generated.

items.question: What do you see as a fundamental limitation of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)?
items.object: The limits of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
items.answer:
I guess one of the fundamental limitations of RLHF is that you don't actually know if the model has learned the thing you want to teach it, right? You have no guarantees that the model has learned what you have taught it. There are a variety of papers that have shown that you can take any of these large language models and, just by adding some additional prompts, it's very easy to make them elicit behavior that you would have hoped you had made the models forget. An exact issue, a big issue, with RLHF is that the reward function just nudges the model toward doing something you wanted it to do. It doesn't necessarily guarantee that your model has learned this.
On the other hand, you could say that human learning also—you as a teacher kind of nudge a student with “this is the response you want, this is not the response you want,” but you don't necessarily know if the person has actually learned the thing you wanted them to learn. Maybe they just copied equations you've given them.

items.question: How do you understand the use of one language model to evaluate another model’s responses for reinforcement learning?
items.object: Reinforcement learning from AI feedback
items.answer: When you do RLHF, what happens is your model will generate different outputs, and then people will say, “This is good, this is not good.” In a very similar vein, I can imagine having two language models. One language model generates the answer, and then you give the other language model maybe the ground-truth answer and the question, and now it can assess how good the generated answer is. First, does it match the ground-truth answer? Then it can check the reasoning: does the reasoning make sense to the language model? That's a very simplistic version of RL from AI feedback, and there are a variety of different ways to make it much more sophisticated.

items.question: Why do you see multi-agent debate as a useful way to improve a language model’s training data?
items.object: Multi-agent debate for improving language-model training data
items.answer: One way that I've been working on a lot is this idea of using multi-agent debate. You have multiple instances of your language model generate different possible answers to the question. It's kind of like when you're trying to solve a math problem or answer a question, you have different thoughts in your mind, and each of these voices in your mind talks to each other. Each of these language models talks to each other, trying to see: Is this answer consistent with my first thought? Is it consistent with my second thought? You can imagine having these language models debate with each other, and then the answer you get at the end of this debate should be a more accurate answer than the original answer. This gets you better data, and then you can use this data to retrain your model. The core idea is basically you can use the model to get better data. You generate from your model, and then you can impose some structure on this generation process to encourage the model to do a bit more reasoning or causal chain of events. At the end, the answer you get is an improved version of what the model would originally generate, so it gives you some improvement operation.

items.question: What do you see as the simplest way to give a language model ground-truth information so it can evaluate another model’s answer?
items.object: Prompting a language model to evaluate an answer against ground truth
items.answer: I’d probably just give it as a prompt. You can ask the first language model, “Here's a question; generate an answer,” and then the second language model—you give the original question again, and then you give the generated answer, and then you say, “Here's the ground-truth answer,” and you can instruct the language model to reflect and describe what is correct or not correct about the answers.
quotes: Probably the simplest way is to just give it as a prompt.

You can ask the first language model, “Here's a question; generate an answer,” and then the second language model—you give the original question again, and then you give the generated answer, and then you say, “Here's the ground-truth answer,” and you can instruct the language model to reflect and describe what is correct or not correct about the answers.

rubrics.text: The response proposes prompting an evaluating language model to assess a generated answer against a ground-truth answer supplied in the prompt.

items.question: What value do you see in using a second language model to give feedback on another model’s reasoning?
items.object: Using a second language model to provide feedback on another model’s reasoning
items.answer: Let's say the first model generates “2 plus 2 is equal to 5.” I'd give the second model the same question, “What is 2 plus 2?” and then the ground-truth answer, four, and then the answer generated by agent: “2 plus 2 equals 5.” Then I can say, “Can you check if this answer is correct and provide feedback on what portions were correct or incorrect?” One thing I could do is feed the intermediate generations of the language model, because the language model generates the answer step by step. I can give it the first sentence and say, “Is this consistent with the right answer?” I can give it the second sentence and say, “Is that consistent?” I can get much richer annotations than just “This is correct” or “This is not correct,” which in principle is something you could also do with people, but it's very tedious for people to do this. In practice, most of the time the RLHF feedback that you get is just a score over the entire output.

items.question: Why do you want to automate reinforcement learning from AI feedback as much as possible?
items.object: Reinforcement learning from AI feedback
items.answer: In this debate procedure that I was talking about earlier, there is no human oversight. One big thing about RL from AI feedback is this idea that you do not want humans to be the bottleneck. LLMs and all these models can be accelerated very quickly on hardware accelerators, but people operate at a specific speed; they're expensive, maybe they're inaccurate. The goal would be to completely automate this as much as possible.

items.question: How do you think a reviewing LLM can judge whether another LLM's answer is satisfactory?
items.object: LLMs evaluating other LLMs' answers in reinforcement learning from AI feedback
items.answer: I think there are two ideas. One idea is that you could give the ground-truth LLM the correct answer. If there are a set of problems that you want to teach the LLM to be more accurate on, you could generate a bunch of questions, get a bunch of answers, and use the LM to critique your answers. The thing that a lot of people want is to assume that you do not have the ground-truth answer. Let's say I want to write a proof for a mathematical theorem. I don't know the ground-truth answer, but I can check to see if someone else's answer is incorrect. I can clearly look at the first step and say, “Well, this step is logical” or “This step is not logical.” I can check the second step. One thought about RL from AI feedback is, in the same way people can prove mathematical proofs by sequentially checking and making sure everything is correct to your knowledge, you can imagine each of these LLMs checking each other: Is every single step correct? If every single step is rational and you get the answer you want at the end, even if you don't know what the ground-truth answer is, we still know this is a satisfactory answer or this is not a satisfactory answer. You can imagine it's a way to search through the space of possible solutions.

items.question: How do you think generating multiple answers helps a critic detect problems in an LLM's response when the correct answer isn't known?
items.object: Multiple model generations as a way to detect inconsistencies in LLM answers
items.answer: I think this is where, in some of my work on RL from AI feedback, I had this idea of having multiple models. If you only have a single answer, if I ask you when this person was born and then the LM just makes up some number, there's no way to verify if it's correct or not. But the thing about LLMs is they can generate multiple answers for a question. If I ask the LLM when this person was born and it gives me 1876, and then it tells me 1896, and it tells me 1895, now you have multiple different answers. Your critic can say, “Clearly something's amiss here, because none of these answers are consistent with each other.” When you introduce this idea of not just having one model generate, but having multiple instances of the model generate different solutions, then you can verify issues with the causality or the chain of reasoning of language models. You can identify things that are logically inconsistent by just having multiple generations come out.

items.question: Why do you see language as a desirable medium for debate between language models?
items.object: Language-based debate between language models
items.answer: For the work that I've been working on, debate, you actually have the language models generate language outputs explicitly, and then each of the language models takes in these language outputs from other models and gives feedback on that. It's purely in the language space. Probably it could be more efficient to be able to do it in some type of vector space, but there are desirable properties to having it in language. If you can have all these agents reasoning in language, we can understand what the agents are doing. It's a hard constraint that forces the model to be reasonable in a sense, because if you do something in some abstract space, you as a person have no idea what the model is doing, and it might also find all types of cheating ways to communicate. Having all of this self-improvement be directly in language is desirable.

items.question: Why do you think language models tend to converge on one answer when they debate each other?
items.object: Convergence in debates between language models
items.answer: Most of the time you end up converging to the same answer, or converging to one answer. I think this might be due to the fact that the models have been trained to converse with people in such a way that they're not very stubborn. If a person constantly suggests the answer, they will respond to it. When you try to repurpose this mechanism to have multiple models talk to each other, the models are very deferential to other models, so almost all the time they will converge to one answer.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between using multi-model debate during training and using it to improve answers after a language model has been trained?
items.object: Multi-model debate as a training strategy and a test-time method
items.answer: In the paper we wrote about this, we primarily focused on this application where you finish training this model, and then this is a way to get better answers from the language model. But one thing that I'm very excited about is this idea that this is also an improvement operator during training time. This is a way to get RL from AI feedback. I've recently been talking to several companies that have also been training large language models, and they're exploring these strategies. It could be either. In general, I think anything that you can do for RL from AI feedback, each of these strategies gives you some mechanism for how good an answer is. You can always use that as a test-time thing as well as a training thing. I think they're two flips of the same coin; I don't think one is very different than the other.

items.question: Why do you think reinforcement learning from AI feedback could cover a wider range of prompts than human feedback?
items.object: The potential coverage of reinforcement learning from AI feedback
items.answer: Ideally any type of RL from AI feedback would be able to apply on arbitrary prompts. You construct this interface that all the models can autonomously talk to each other and generate answers. As long as the models can autonomously generate answers, you can give it all types of prompts. One issue with having people rate the accuracy of something is it's really hard to rate the accuracy of not-so-well-known people, because you would have to search for ages on Google, and maybe to verify one passage that's generated you need to spend two hours. So it's not very scalable, and for lots of prompts maybe there's just no easy way to do it. If you have this AI feedback and it can give you answers for everything, you would hope that the coverage is actually a lot more than the coverage you could get from human feedback.

items.question: How do you think language-model improvement should be measured as models become more capable?
items.object: Evaluating language-model improvement through benchmarks and multi-agent competition
items.answer: What you would see is maybe on this benchmark it used to be 60%, now it goes to 80%. You would want to see these consistent improvements across a wide variety of benchmarks. There is a question: let's say the models get really good—which I think they're very, very far away from at the moment—but if they were to get very, very good and maybe do perfectly at all these human benchmarks, how do you assess the performance of these models? There's a nice idea from multi-agent debate. You can use something like an Elo rating system. For chess and Go, there are bots much better than people, but we can still quantify how much better they are by pitting these agents against each other. If an agent is able to beat another agent 100% of the time, then it's probably a much more intelligent agent than the original one. The hope is that if you use this type of multi-agent competition as your improvement operator, you can use the ease with which the language model is able to generate solutions to convince another agent as a measure of how intelligent it is. As a model gets more and more intelligent, ideally it would blow away the other model. Maybe that could be a metric for improvement at that point. But I think that's very speculative. The models right now are very, very far away from human level, and probably in the next year or upcoming several years we'll have plenty of benchmarks to see numbers go up a little.

As a model gets more and more intelligent, ideally it would blow away the other model. Maybe that could be a metric for improvement at that point. But I think that's very speculative. The models right now are very, very far away from human level, and probably in the next year or upcoming several years we'll have plenty of benchmarks to see numbers go up a little.

items.question: How do you interpret the improvements you have seen in your research on language-model debate?
items.object: The significance and limitations of improvements in Du's debate research
items.answer: In our research, I see like a 20% improvement, which is a decent amount. We wrote this paper in May, and there have been several follow-ups. Some of the large companies, for example Anthropic, might also be exploring debate. It seems like there's a boost, but we don't have access to the large language models, so we actually cannot do this full-on training at a large scale. We don't see these new capabilities or anything like that; that would be the hope. Right now we see this in the raw numbers.

items.question: How do you think limited access to proprietary language model weights affects your research and the pace of improvement?
items.object: Access to proprietary language model weights and its effect on research
items.answer:
We have API access to these models, as everyone else does. This way we proposed to do RL from AI feedback doesn't require the weights of the network. We can directly use it; it's more of a test-time thing, where you can still use this to improve your performance at test time. But the big issue is we can't fine-tune the model or use that to improve their performance.

I think that's a bit unfortunate because there is a pretty large gap at the moment between all these open-source models and the ones being used commercially. It feels like the pace of research or the pace of improvement could be improved a lot if the weights were made available to everyone. But there's so much money and commercial interest on this side that that's unlikely to happen.

items.question: How do you assess Llama 2 as a model for debate and AI feedback research?
items.object: Llama 2's capabilities and suitability for debate and AI feedback research
items.answer:
The issue with Llama 2 is it's still pretty poor at the moment. Lots of people talk about how it's really good, but some peers claim that if you use Llama 2 and do lots of fine-tuning, it can match GPT-3.5 performance. What we find is it can match GPT-3.5 performance on one task, which is a task they spent the last month optimizing for, and it's far worse on every other task. Even GPT-3.5—for this debate stuff and a lot of this AI feedback stuff, GPT-4 is much better at this than 3.5 is. If you're stuck with things that are much worse than 3.5, it's very hard to get improvements.

One thing that was kind of interesting is that after we released this paper, another group of people tried it on these open-source models and also noticed the improvement.

items.question: How do you think about the prospects for open-source language models catching up with proprietary models from companies like OpenAI?
items.object: The gap between open-source and proprietary language models
items.answer:
I do think at the moment there's a pretty massive gap between the open-source language models and the internal ones. I think a huge reason for this gap is actually data. OpenAI has spent a lot of time gathering very customized data to make that agent look very appealing to people.

I think this lack of data feels like it's possible to overcome. OpenAI and Anthropic, which I guess was from OpenAI, were doing this large language model scaling for four or five years, and also trying to commercialize it for the last 2.5 years. Everyone else kind of suddenly realized they had to do this maybe around nine months ago. So I think there's a big time difference at the moment. The open-source models are much worse. I think even the company models—I don't know any information about this—Facebook's model internally is probably much worse than the open ones. A lot of it is just time. I would hope that maybe in a year or two, or maybe even in one year, things will catch up.

People constantly say they feel like there's a lot of technical knowledge to train these models, and that's one reason why OpenAI is so much better than the other ones. I actually don't think that's the case. There are a couple things people don't appreciate about training the models. One big one is tuning, finding hyperparameters on smaller models and having the exact same hyperparameter scale for larger ones. Besides a few technical tricks, I think the main thing missing right now is just the data. Because it's just the data, I feel like maybe in a year or two people should catch up. I don't think there's technical knowledge that's missing.

items.question: How do you think open-source generative AI could overcome the barrier of GPU costs?
items.object: GPU costs as a barrier to open-source generative AI
items.answer: I think that could be a barrier. It is true that the GPU cost is quite large, probably several million, maybe even 100 million, maybe hundreds of millions, maybe even a billion for huge models. Maybe we need some type of research center or something like this, or a government-funded thing. With particle accelerators and particle physics, you have the Large Hadron Collider, and that's hundreds of millions of dollars or more. If we had an equal-sized effort, I think you could totally do this.

items.question: How do you assess the open-source community's claim that a small model with a little fine-tuning can match leading models?
items.object: Claims that small, lightly fine-tuned open-source models can match leading models
items.answer: I do feel like at the moment there's a disconnect between what people are—there's a big disconnect between what people constantly say online right now in the open-source community, like, “You just need a small model, you just need to fine-tune it a little, and then it will reach their performance,” and the actual performance. People maybe should focus a bit more on using more GPUs. That could be problematic.

items.question: Why do you believe physical embodiment is essential to artificial intelligence?
items.object: The physical AI hypothesis and robotics
items.answer: Throughout my PhD I've been very interested in the idea of artificial intelligence. To have artificial intelligence, we really need to have it physically in the world. We need an agent that can visually understand the world, physically act in the world, have intents in the world, and interact with other agents. I really believe in this physical AI hypothesis. Robotics is basically the instantiation of having a physically intelligent AI agent.

items.question: How do you imagine multi-agent debate could help construct an intelligent robot?
items.object: Multi-agent debate across multimodal models in robotics
items.answer: This multi-agent debate stuff is one way to try to get a more intelligent AI. This idea in general could be applied in different ways. Right now it's just on language models, but you can imagine different models in the robot processing system. Maybe you have a video generation model that generates possible actions you want to do. You have some type of action model that takes images and predicts actions you want. You can imagine each of these models talking with each other: the action model says, “You gave me this image. This image is not possible. Go please refine it a little.” You can imagine having a network of these individual modules that are all talking with each other, and when you have a set of these decentralized models all talking with each other, maybe that whole thing can be some distributed operating system to construct an intelligent robot. I feel like this idea of debate or self-improvement could be broadly applied across multimodal models on a robot also.

items.question: How do you assess the role of hardware limitations in holding back progress in robotics?
items.object: Hardware and intelligence as barriers to progress in robotics
items.answer:
I agree that hardware for robots is a lot worse than what people have. We don't have tactile sensing. The arms are very awkward to use; they are very constrained. But when you give a person a remote control of the robot, they can do a lot of tasks in the kitchen. Almost every task you can imagine you can actually do by remotely controlling the robot.

Those are big issues, but it feels like we're also missing the fundamental intelligent portion. As a person, I can do a lot more than I can autonomously code my robot to do at the moment. If we could do more autonomously with the robots, people would be much more interested in robotics. Then we would have the interest in hardware to get better hardware to train robots. I think the thing is there's no proof of concept of AI working in robotics still, and that makes it so people aren't very interested in trying to get better hardware for the robots.

items.question: What do you find interesting about building a society of small AI agents that talk to each other?
items.object: A decentralized society of AI agents
items.answer: Everyone is working on these very giant monolithic models that can do everything; they can sense, they can perceive, and stuff like this. But I feel like our brain is actually very decentralized. We have areas for motor control, vision, memory. It's cool to think about having not a single AI, but a society of AIs in your mind. You have a bunch of different small agents talking to each other, and that's how you actually function. You have one thought process that's trying to remember things you're doing, another one that perceives what you're doing. I think that's an interesting idea that maybe people would also find interesting to think about.

items.question: Why do you currently see academia as a better place than industry for pursuing your research interests?
items.object: Academic versus industry research freedom
items.answer:
If you had asked me this maybe one or two years ago, I would have been a lot less certain, because at the time it felt like you could do very open-ended research both in industry as well as in academia. Nowadays, because there's so much commercial success with these models, the research you can do in industry is actually very limited. If you want to work on RL agents without any language model, you can't really do that. There's a huge push for you to work on RL for language models.

During the summer I was working at Google; earlier I was working at Facebook. I've generally been playing a lot with these vision-language models. They still seem very far away from actual intelligence on the vision side. But even if you don't believe that a single large language model will solve everything, which I don't know—I've been playing around—but if you don't believe in this hypothesis, you still have to work on this because that's the vogue theme, and people think that it's so promising commercially.
